stories.title: 'If you started running, they shot you' - inside Nigeria's growing kidnapping crisis
stories.summary: "If you ran into a room, they set the room on fire," says Fatima, describing a recent attack on her village in Zamfara, north-western Nigeria. "If you came out and started running, they shot you." The gunmen, who struck at 02:00, split into groups to surround residents: one at the village entrance, one in the centre and one at the back. "They opened fire without a care in the world, shooting indiscriminately," the 55-year-old quietly tells the BBC World Service. It was one of many attacks that have caused havoc in the mainly Muslim community where residents live in fear of being kidnapped for ransom. Fatima explains how the raids unfold: "You could have 100 motorcycles, and each one could be carrying three people." About 70 people, including children, were killed from the village of Bia Buki in June, according to Fatima. She describes how the attackers also targeted villagers as they fled and children were injured falling into ditches. Among the dead were her husband and six of his seven siblings. Fatima is one of an estimated 800,000 Nigerians who the UN says have been displaced in the country's north-west. One of the main reasons people have left their homes is violence. Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by gangs, locally referred to as bandits, who often move around on motorcycles and attack quickly then ride away, escaping before security forces arrive.

stories.title: Iceland holds knife-edge referendum on EU - and it could be decided on fish
stories.summary: Inside a waterfront factory, workers in hairnets and blue overalls are sorting freshly caught cod and haddock, and machines process the fish into fillets, mostly bound for Europe. Visir fishing boss Pétur Pálsson, who fears joining the European Union would cost Iceland jobs and drive factories abroad, says: "If we are in the EU, they will be the ones who make the policy." On Saturday, voters in this island nation of almost 400,000 people will decide whether their country should resume talks on joining the EU. It is a referendum that polls suggest is too close to call. Supporters think closer European ties could help tame Iceland's volatile currency and soaring cost of living. Opponents say Iceland's sovereignty and control over "priceless" fishing waters are at stake, and would rather continue going it alone. It is a fault line that has divided Icelanders for decades, but after winning a snap election in 2024 Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir's centre-left government pledged to hold a referendum by 2027. Russia's war in Ukraine, sharpening Arctic rivalries and US President Donald Trump's tariff threats and designs on Greenland have accelerated that timetable. "Things have been moving very rapidly with respect to geopolitical challenges," Finance Minister Daði Már Kristófersson tells the BBC, pushing Iceland's place in the world "up the agenda". Iceland lies high in the North Atlantic, adjacent to a strategic stretch of sea called the GIUK gap, where Russian maritime activity is closely watched by the West. It is a founding member of Nato, and yet has no military of its own. One poll this week put the Yes vote ahead by 51.3% to 48.7%; an earlier poll had the two camps neck and neck.

stories.title: FDA approves new drug Rasonque to treat advanced pancreatic cancer
stories.summary: The US FDA on Wednesday approved Revolution Medicines' Rasonque for advanced pancreatic cancer, opening a new treatment option for patients with metastatic disease. A large trial found the once-daily pill doubled survival rates, offering fresh hope for people who have exhausted other treatments.
